newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's surgery options may be simple or risky.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's surgery options may be simple or risky.

text.p: The revelation that Boris Yeltsin's forthcoming heart operation is to be a bypass was meant to show a new openness about the Kremlin leader's health.

But the range of different types of bypass means that those outside the narrow group of doctors and officials involved in organising the operation are still in the dark as to the seriousness of his ailment and the risks involved.
The delay in carrying out the operation -- the 65-year-old president told the nation on September 5 that he would have it at the end of the month -- has only added to the confusion.

Leo Bokeria, the director of one of Russia's leading heart clinics, said on Friday that Yeltsin, who doctors say suffers from problems with the blood supply to his heart, could be undergoing pre-surgical treatment.

Speaking in an interview at the Bakuleva Scientific Centre of Cardiovascular Surgery, he said that the weaker a patient's heart contractions the more pre-surgical treatment was needed and the more dangerous the operation.
But he said the delay could only be for extra consultations.
Michael Rees, cardio-radiologist at Bristol Royal Infirmary, said surgery would normally take place as soon as possible, although it could take two or three days to prepare.

"A delay implies that something has to be corrected before surgery," he said by telephone. "It could be that in testing they discovered something that they had to take account of in the surgery, and there are many of those."

Doctors could have discovered any one of a myriad of conditions which needed to be put right before surgery, expected to be done in Moscow. "That could be a whole medical textbook," he said, citing diabetes, blood pressure or kidney problems.
Or they could be weaning Yeltsin off a course of drugs.
"If he had been on a long course of steroids, for example, you would have to stop the steroids well before surgery. He had been looking puffy and that could point to steroids," Rees said.
Like Bokeria, Rees also said the doctors could need the time merely to gather and prepare the medical team and equipment.
The presidential press office said on Friday that two top German cardiologists would join the Russian team of experts, who are expected to decide on September 28 when to do the operation.
Russian media said on Thursday that pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey would join the team, although DeBakey himself said he had not yet been approached.
Bokeria said that overall the U.S. record on bypass operations was better than Russia's but he said that Moscow's top institutions were internationally competitive.
He saw no problem with inviting foreign specialists. "It's normal, I don't think anyone minds," said Bokeria, adding that he was not offended not to have been asked to take part.
"It's a huge responsibility...I do surgery four days a week...it's routine work for me but this one is really unusual," said the grey-haired surgeon, dressed in his cap and robe.

When it came to the surgery itself, there were many options, including laser treatment, angioplasty -- using a balloon to unblock vessels -- or the riskier but longer-lasting option of shunting all the diseased vessels in open heart surgery.
"There are many possibilities but it depends on what is possible with the patient," he said.
If the heart was contracting well, the chances of survival were 96 to 98 percent. If not, they could be much worse, he said. Possible post-surgical problems were also manifold.
"There are many types of complications because any (bodily) system could be involved if surgery is done incorrectly or if a patient has problems before surgery," said Bokeria.

The recovery period could vary between several days and a couple of months, although he stressed that without having examined Yeltsin or seen his medical records he had little to go on. The president might even have been operated on already.
"There is a rumour in Russia that he was. That's quite possible but I really don't know," he said.
